scene.note: The clipboard's numbers become typed variables in Clipboard.java, the compiler checks each value fits its type, and the program prints the count.

steps.note: The top of the clipboard names the crossing the Linnet makes.
Under Task 1 you keep that text in a variable with the type for text.
The compiler checks that the value really is text in double quotes.
The program prints what the variable holds.
This morning the clipboard says how many seats the boat has.
The seats left start at that number, taken by its name, not typed in.
A count of seats is a whole number, and the compiler checks it is one.
The terminal shows the seats left before anyone boards.
Some passengers board, and the clipboard notes how many.
The seats left get a new value: the seats there were, less the passengers who boarded.
The same variable holds a new value now. It is changed, not made again.
The terminal shows the count before and after boarding.
The clipboard has the price of a single crossing, in pounds and pence.
Under Task 4 the price goes in a variable whose type keeps the part after the point.
A type for whole numbers would lose the pence, and the compiler refuses to squeeze it in.
The program prints the fare.
Ossian's lines keep the skipper and the boat in variables called a and b.
Each gets a name that says what it holds, where it is made and everywhere it is used.
A name missed in one place shows up as a name the compiler cannot find.
The program prints the same two lines as before.
